units.name: glob-matching
units.role: Compile shell-style glob patterns into fast path matchers and match many globs against one path in a single pass.
units.description: This is the pattern language engine for file names and paths. Someone writes a pattern with stars, question marks, brace groups or character ranges; this unit reads that miniature language, complains clearly about malformed patterns such as an unclosed bracket or a dangling escape, and turns each pattern into something that can be tested against a candidate path very quickly. Its second job is bulk matching: given thousands of patterns it sorts them into cheap buckets (plain names, plain extensions, common prefixes and suffixes, and only then true regular expressions) so that checking one path against the whole collection costs about one hash lookup, and it reports which patterns matched, by position, not merely whether any did. It must never touch the disk, the network, the clock or the environment: it only transforms text and answers yes, no or which questions, so the same patterns and the same path always give the same answer. Deciding what a match means, such as skipping a folder or choosing a decompression tool, belongs entirely to its callers.

units.role: Decide, for a single path, whether ignore-file rules, user glob overrides or file-type selections say to skip it.
units.description: This unit holds the meaning of the rules that decide which files a search should skip or keep. It knows how to read an ignore file line by line and turn each line into a rule: a leading exclamation mark flips the rule into a keep-this-after-all exception, a trailing slash means the rule only applies to folders, a leading slash anchors the rule to the folder holding the ignore file, comments and blank lines are skipped, and when several rules apply the last matching one wins. It applies the same line semantics, inverted, to globs the user types on the command line, so those act as an explicit include and exclude list. It also owns the built-in dictionary mapping a friendly type name such as rust or cpp to the file name patterns that define it, and the machinery to add, select, negate or clear those types. It additionally locates the machine-wide git excludes file by consulting environment variables and the user's git configuration. What it must never do is walk directories, open the files being searched, or decide the overall search plan: it answers one question at a time about one path and hands back the verdict along with which rule was responsible.

units.name: directory-walker
units.role: Recursively walk directory trees, serially or in parallel, applying the per-directory ignore-rule stack and yielding surviving files.
units.description: This unit decides which files on disk are worth looking at. Given one or more starting paths it descends through every subfolder, and at each level it reads the rule files it finds there and stacks those rules on top of the rules inherited from parent folders. Every file or folder it meets is checked against that stack and against simpler filters: is it hidden, is it too deep or too shallow, is it larger than the allowed size, is it on a different disk, is it a symbolic link we were told not to follow, is it the very file we are writing our own output to. Everything that survives is handed back one entry at a time, either through a plain one-at-a-time iterator or through a pool of worker threads that share work with each other. It also offers a second mode that answers the same question about a single path handed to it out of the blue, remembering rule stacks it has already compiled so repeat questions are cheap. It must never look inside a file's contents, and it must never silently swallow errors: an unreadable folder, an unparsable rule file or a loop of symbolic links is reported alongside the results rather than crashing the walk.

units.name: matcher-interface
units.role: Define the abstract search contract every regex engine implements and every consumer programs against.
units.description: This is the shared rulebook that lets ripgrep search text without caring which pattern-matching engine does the work. It spells out what any engine must be able to do: given a block of text and a starting position, report where the next match begins and ends; optionally report the sub-pieces of a match, meaning the parenthesised groups people write in patterns; optionally say which bytes can never appear in a match, or which character ends a line, so the rest of the program can take shortcuts. It supplies the small vocabulary everyone shares: a match is a start and end pair that can never run backwards, a line ending is either one byte or the two-byte Windows sequence, and a byte set is a compact yes-or-no table over all possible byte values. On top of the bare minimum an engine must supply, it provides ready-made versions of everything else: looping over all matches, stopping early when the caller says so, skipping empty matches so the loop always makes progress, and rewriting matched text using a replacement template. It is deliberately pure bookkeeping over bytes already in memory: it must never open a file, touch the network, read the clock, run another program, or assume any particular regex library exists.

units.name: regex-matcher
units.role: Turn user pattern text plus search flags into a compiled, line-aware matcher over the default regex engine.
units.description: This unit understands what a search pattern means. It takes the raw pattern text the user typed, one pattern or many, together with the switches that modify its meaning, such as ignore case, smart case, whole word, whole line, treat the pattern as plain text, allow matches to span lines, Windows line endings, and Unicode on or off, and produces a ready-to-use matcher the rest of the program can ask where the next match is. Along the way it inspects the structure of the pattern to make searching faster and safer: it works out whether the pattern contains capital letters, which is how smart case decides; it pulls out fixed pieces of text that must be present in any match so a cheap scan can skip lines that cannot possibly match; it works out which bytes can never appear in a match so whole files can be skipped; it rewrites the pattern so it can never match across a line boundary when searching line by line, and reports a clear error when that rewrite is impossible; and it refuses patterns containing a byte the caller has banned. It must never read files, touch the network, or perform the search itself. Its shortcuts are allowed to raise false alarms that the full engine then rejects, but must never cause a real match to be missed.

units.description: This is the second of the two search engines ripgrep can use to decide whether text matches the user's pattern. The default engine is fast but deliberately refuses certain fancy pattern features; this one hands the pattern to a long-established pattern-matching library written in C, which supports extras such as backreferences and look-around, at the cost of being slower and, on pathological patterns, dramatically slower. Its job is to translate ripgrep's user-facing options, including case sensitivity, smart case, whole word or whole line, treat-as-plain-text, multiline and Unicode mode, into the equivalent settings of that library, to join multiple patterns into one, to compile the pattern and optionally have the library generate native machine code for it, and then to answer the same questions the rest of ripgrep asks of any engine. It must never print anything, touch files, or decide which files to search, and it must never silently change the meaning of the user's pattern: everything it wraps around the pattern is driven strictly by the flags it was given. It is built into ripgrep only when the optional feature is switched on.

units.role: Line-oriented search driver: apply a matcher to a haystack and report matches, context lines and binary events to a caller-supplied receiver.
units.description: This unit performs the actual search over the contents of a file or stream once someone else has decided which file to look at and which pattern to look for. It takes a chunk of bytes, decides where each line begins and ends including different line endings and optional character-encoding conversion, asks the pattern matcher whether a line matches, and then decides what the caller should be told about: the matching lines themselves, the requested number of lines before and after each match, the gaps between separated groups of context, every line when passthrough is on, the inverse when inverted matching is on, and matches that span several lines when multiline mode is on. It also counts line numbers and byte offsets, enforces limits such as stop after so many matches or stop at the first non-matching line, and notices when the data looks like binary rubbish so the search can be halted or the offending bytes replaced. It never formats output itself and never decides which files to visit: it hands every result to a callback and lets the printer decide how it looks. It must not colour, filter by file name, or report offsets inconsistent with what it handed to that callback.

units.name: search-input
units.role: Supply bytes to the searcher: a rolling whole-line buffer over any reader, plus the policy for memory-mapping files.
units.description: This is the plumbing that gets the raw contents of a file, or of anything else readable such as piped input, in front of the search logic. It has two halves. The first is a rolling buffer: it reads a chunk of data at a time into a fixed-size scratch area and guarantees that whatever it hands upward always ends exactly at the end of a line, never in the middle of one. If a single line is too long to fit it grows the scratch area, unless the caller asked for a memory cap, in which case it stops and reports that the cap was exceeded. As it reads, it can watch for a byte that signals the data is not human-readable text and either stop right there, pretending the file ended, or quietly replace that byte with a line break so the rest can still be searched; either way the suspicious byte never reaches the search logic, and it remembers where such data was first seen. The second half is the memory-map decision: given an open file it decides whether the operating system should map that file straight into memory or whether ordinary reads should be used, refusing unless the caller explicitly opted in, and reporting a plain no rather than failing when mapping is impossible. It must never interpret the data: it does no matching and writes nothing to the user's output.

units.role: Render search results into the human-readable path-line-text output, the count and file-list summaries, and the machine-readable record stream.
units.description: This unit decides what a search result actually looks like when it reaches you. When the search engine finds a matching line it hands the raw bytes and offsets here, and this unit chooses how to lay them out: the file name, the line number and column, the matched text with the matching part highlighted in colour, the surrounding context lines, and the separators between chunks. It also produces the shorter answers: just a count of matches per file, or just the list of file names that did or did not contain a match. For other programs rather than people, it can emit one record per event so results can be consumed reliably. Along the way it interprets the user's colour preferences, tidies up file paths for display, optionally substitutes matched text with a user-supplied replacement, and tallies statistics such as how many matches, lines, files and bytes were involved and how long searching took. It writes only to the destination it is handed: it must never open or read files itself, never decide which files get searched, and never alter the bytes it reports beyond the formatting and replacement it was explicitly asked to perform.

units.name: hyperlink-formatting
units.role: Parse hyperlink format strings and named shortcuts, then fill in path, line, column and machine name to make clickable terminal links.
units.description: This is ripgrep's rulebook for turning a search hit into something you can click on in your terminal. The user says what shape a link should have, either by writing a template naming slots for the path, line and column, or by naming a shortcut such as the one for a particular editor. This unit reads that template, checks it makes sense (it must begin with a proper web-address scheme, it must contain a slot for the path, and it cannot ask for a column without also asking for a line) and produces a friendly error listing the available shortcuts when it does not. Later, for each printed result, it fills the slots in: the machine name and any compatibility-layer prefix come from a small environment record set once at startup, while the file path, line number and column come from the individual match. The path is turned into an absolute, percent-encoded web address so that spaces and odd characters survive. Finally it wraps the printed text in the invisible escape codes terminals understand as a link. It must never invent a link when no format was given, when the output does not support links, or when colour is switched off, and it must never leave a link open that it did not open. It also does not look up the machine name itself; someone else must hand it that.

units.name: search-index
units.role: Experimental on-disk index: locate and open the index database, and reduce a pattern to the literal fragments a matching file must contain.
units.description: This is an unfinished, experimental part of ripgrep meant to make repeat searches much faster by remembering ahead of time which short chunks of text appear in which files. It has two halves. The first finds and opens the index storage: it looks for a hidden index folder by walking upward from the current folder toward the top of the disk, or uses a path named by an environment variable if one is set, and then creates or opens a small embedded database file inside it, either read-only for searching or read-write for building. The second half is pure reasoning about patterns: it takes a parsed pattern and works out a yes-and-or-no formula of short literal strings that any file containing a match must contain, so files failing the formula could be skipped. It must never change what a search reports: the formula is only ever allowed to be over-permissive, proposing extra candidate files, never to exclude a file that could really match, and giving up and proposing everything is always the safe answer. In the code as it stands the two halves are not yet wired together, and the caller only opens the database before falling back to an ordinary exhaustive search.

units.name: preprocessing
units.role: Turn a file into searchable text by running an external program, either a decompressor or a user-supplied helper, and streaming its output.
units.description: This is ripgrep's bridge to other programs on the machine. Before ripgrep searches a file, this unit can hand that file to a helper program and read back whatever the helper prints, so the search sees plain text instead of the raw bytes on disk. It does this in two ways. First, it keeps a built-in table matching file name patterns to decompression tools, so compressed files of the common kinds are unpacked on the fly. Second, it provides the general machinery for launching any command and reading its output as it is produced, which is what backs the user's own helper program. It is careful about failure: it looks a program up on the system search path first so a stray program in the current folder can never be run by accident, it drains the helper's error output on a separate thread so a chatty program cannot deadlock, and if the helper exits unhappily it turns the helper's own error text into a readable message. If no decompressor matches a file, or the matching tool is not installed, it quietly falls back to reading the file as it is. What it must never do is decide which files get searched, filter or ignore paths, or interpret the contents: it only produces a stream of bytes for someone else to search.

units.name: cli-io
units.role: Terminal and standard-stream plumbing: tty detection, buffered colour-capable output, pattern-file reading, byte escaping, size parsing and machine-name lookup.
units.description: This is the layer that lets ripgrep talk to the terminal and to raw text the user supplies. It answers questions such as: is our output going to a real terminal window or being piped into a file, so should we flush every line and allow colour, or write in big fast blocks? Is data waiting on the input stream, so we should read that instead of scanning the current folder? It reads lists of search patterns out of a file or off the input stream, one per line, and when a line is not valid text it reports exactly which file, which line and which byte was bad rather than failing cryptically. It converts awkward characters both ways, turning raw bytes such as a line break into a typeable form and typed sequences back into real bytes, so a user can express any byte at a shell prompt. It parses friendly size strings into an exact number of bytes, and it asks the operating system for the machine's name when building clickable links. It is deliberately ignorant about searching: it must never decide what to search for, interpret patterns, match files, or format results. Its only job is faithful, well-explained input and output at the edges of the program.

units.name: cli-flags
units.role: Authoritative definition of every command-line flag, plus the parser that turns raw arguments and a config file into a flat validated record.
units.description: This unit is ripgrep's contract with the person typing at the terminal. One file holds a single giant catalogue with an entry for every option ripgrep accepts: its long name, its optional one-letter name, any aliases, any undo form, which help section it belongs to, its short and long documentation, what kind of value it takes, and crucially what it changes when supplied. A second file is the parser: it walks the words the user actually typed, decides whether each is a flag, a value belonging to a flag, or a plain file or pattern argument, looks the flag up in the catalogue and asks that entry to record the change; if the user typed something that is not a real flag, it works out which real flags look most similar and suggests them. A third file is the resulting record, one field per setting, holding literally what was asked for and nothing more. A fourth handles a configuration file named by an environment variable, treating each non-comment line as one extra argument placed before the user's own so that typed arguments always win. The unit deliberately only validates and never acts: it does not open the files being searched, build patterns, run other programs, or check whether output is a terminal. That keeps parsing fast and keeps help and version working even when the surrounding environment is broken.

units.role: Composition root: turn the parsed flat record of user flags into the concrete configured matcher, searcher, printer, walker and worker.
units.description: This is where ripgrep decides what the user actually meant. It receives a flat, literal record of everything typed on the command line and turns it into the real working parts of a search: which pattern engine to use and how it should treat case, word boundaries, line endings and Unicode; which kind of output to produce and with which colours, separators and clickable links; how the file-finding walk should behave with respect to hidden files, ignore rules, type filters, symbolic links, depth and size limits; how many threads to use; whether to sort results and by what; how to treat binary files; and whether to run files through a decompressor or a helper program first. It also settles the many implicit rules ripgrep is known for, such as showing line numbers and headings only when writing to a real terminal, searching the current folder when no path is given but reading piped input when there is some, and disabling parallelism whenever sorted output is requested. To make those judgements it must look at the outside world once: it detects whether output is a terminal, resolves the current folder, reads patterns from files or piped input, and may run a helper program to learn the machine name. What it must never do is perform the search, print results, or walk the file system: it only hands out fully configured parts, and it must fail loudly with a clear message when a combination of flags is impossible rather than silently guessing.

units.name: search-orchestration
units.role: Per-file work loop: turn walk entries into things to search, choose how to read each one, and drive matcher, searcher and printer over it.
units.description: This unit decides, for each individual thing ripgrep has been asked to look at, whether it is worth looking at and how to get at its contents. First it takes the raw entries produced by the folder walk and turns them into searchable items, dropping anything that is not a real file such as a folder or a broken link, while always keeping anything the user named explicitly, and optionally trimming a leading current-folder marker from displayed paths. Then, for each item, it picks a reading strategy: read piped input if the item is the input stream, run the user's helper program and read its output, transparently decompress the file if the user asked for that and the file looks compressed, or simply open the file directly, which is the fastest path because it allows memory mapping. It also decides how strict to be about binary files, being lenient for files the user named directly and stricter for files merely discovered by the walk. Finally it hands the chosen data to the search engine together with the chosen pattern engine and output format, and reports back two things: whether anything matched and optional per-file statistics for the caller to add up. It must never decide which paths to visit, never decide what the pattern means, and never format results itself.

units.name: cli-main
units.role: The program's front door: parse the command line, pick a mode, drive the search, choose the exit code.
units.description: This is the piece that runs when someone types the ripgrep command at a terminal. It hands the command line off to be parsed, then looks at what the user asked for and takes one of a handful of paths: print help or version information and stop; print the built-in list of file types and stop; write out a manual page or a shell completion script and stop; list the files that would be searched without searching them; build or read a search index; or, in the normal case, actually search. For searching it walks the set of files, one at a time when a single thread or sorted output was requested and otherwise across many threads at once, asks the search machinery to examine each file, forwards any per-file failure to the error reporter, and optionally prints a summary of counts and elapsed time at the end. Finally it decides the number the program hands back to the shell: zero if something matched, one if nothing matched, two if any error occurred. It has two rules it must never break: a broken pipe, as when output is piped into a pager, must be treated as a graceful successful exit rather than a crash, and a per-file failure must never abort the whole run. It does no pattern matching, no ignore-rule interpretation and no result formatting itself; it only sequences the parts that do.

units.name: diagnostics
units.role: Global switches and error-stream printing for non-fatal messages, ignore-file complaints, and verbose debug logging.
units.description: This is how ripgrep complains. Some problems are fatal, such as an unrecognised option, but most are not: a file it could not open, an ignore file with a malformed line, a configuration file it could not read. Rather than stopping, ripgrep prints a short note to the error stream and carries on. This unit owns three global switches decided once at startup: whether such notes are shown at all, whether the narrower category of ignore-file complaints is shown, and a one-way flag that flips the first time an error note is printed so the program can later report a failure exit status even though it kept running. It also installs the destination for verbose debug and trace lines, formatted with their level, source file and line and sent to the same error stream. A deliberate quirk: before printing to the error stream it briefly takes the lock on the normal output stream so that, when both go to the same terminal, the two kinds of output cannot get shuffled together mid-line. It must never write to normal output, never abort the program for an ordinary message, and never lose the error flag once set, though it does deliberately end the process immediately and successfully if the error stream turns out to be a broken pipe.

units.name: grep-facade
units.role: Umbrella package that re-exports the six ripgrep searching packages under a single namespace.
units.description: This is a one-page front door for the whole ripgrep search library. Ripgrep's searching machinery is split across six separately published packages: one that defines what a text matcher is, one that matches with the default regular-expression engine, one that matches with the alternative engine, one that scans files line by line, one that formats results for the screen or for other programs, and one that handles command-line plumbing such as reading piped input. Rather than making a program list all six by name, this file simply says that when you ask for one of six well-known names, here is the package really meant. It contains no logic, no decisions and no input or output at all: it is seven lines of aliases plus a documentation comment. The alias for the alternative engine is the only conditional one, existing only when ripgrep is compiled with that support turned on. Ripgrep's own program goes through this front door for every one of the six names.

violations_observed.note: The dependency is bidirectional. The hyperlink builder reaches back into search-output's crate-private DecimalFormatter (crates/printer/src/util.rs:415) at mod.rs:551,555, while the printers depend on hyperlink for Interpolator and HyperlinkConfig. DecimalFormatter is a general numeric-formatting helper owned by neither concept; a shared utility unit would break the cycle. Recorded, not fixed.

search-engine's public BinaryDetection is a wrapper whose single field is search-input's crate-private enum; it unwraps that field directly at mod.rs:800 and destructures the enum's payloads at mod.rs:104,114 and core.rs:224-225. Making search-input a real boundary would require publishing BinaryDetection and BufferAllocation.

DEFAULT_BUFFER_CAPACITY and alloc_error are borrowed by the multiline and in-memory search paths (mod.rs:996,1002,1021; glue.rs:120,169) that have nothing to do with the line buffer, so they act as shared crate utilities rather than part of search-input's contract.

pathutil.rs has a split personality: strip_prefix and file_name serve the rule matchers, but the two hidden-file tests exist solely for the walker, and the file imports the walker's DirEntry. The two units therefore depend on each other through this one file. It was assigned to ignore-rules because the rule matchers cannot compile without it.

The Error and Match types that every rule matcher returns, plus the partial-error accumulator, are defined in the walker's lib.rs rather than in the rule files. lib.rs is really a shared vocabulary both units depend on; it was kept with the walker because Error is traversal-flavoured, carrying depth and converting walk errors.

A genuine cycle. The parser calls HiArgs::from_low_args to produce its result type, while the wiring unit consumes LowArgs and every value type the parser produces. The seam would be for parse() to return LowArgs and let the caller do the wiring.

flags/mod.rs does double duty: it defines the Flag trait and Category vocabulary that cli-help-docs consumes, and separately re-exports every documentation generator so cli-main reaches them through the flags namespace. That re-export block is the only reason cli-flags appears to depend on cli-help-docs.

cli/src/lib.rs declares the decompression and subprocess modules and re-exports their whole public surface, so the facade for the preprocessing unit is published by a sibling unit. Nothing in cli-io actually calls into preprocessing.

The index dispatch shim was placed in cli-main rather than search-orchestration because it calls back into main.rs's private search functions (enabled.rs:12,14), which would otherwise create a cycle. It also opens an index through HiArgs and immediately discards it, since index-narrowed search is not implemented yet.

The multiline and text suggestion helpers pattern-match on the literal English wording produced by regex-matcher's error formatting, making that message text a de-facto interface even though an ErrorKind enum exists for exactly this purpose and is never matched on.
The exit-code decision reads a program-global errored flag owned by diagnostics rather than a value threaded through return types, so the two units are coupled through shared mutable state.
